title: ExoNotes: do ExoFOP observer notes carry disposition signal beyond the numeric TOI catalogue?
description:
Do the free-text observing notes astronomers write on TESS Objects of Interest carry disposition-relevant information that the numeric catalogue columns do not?

A pre-registered study. Free text is converted to numeric semantic features with a System One model (Jev, TypeSafe AI) used strictly as a featurizer; gradient boosting is the predictor and cross-validation grouped by host star is the arbiter. Model probabilities are never thresholded into a decision.

Result. On 1,482 labelled TOIs across 1,388 host stars, semantic features improve held-out prediction of TFOPWG disposition by ΔAUC +0.0432 (95% CI +0.0324 to +0.0547; AUC 0.9044 → 0.9476) — 5.3× the minimum effect the study was pre-registered to detect. All six pre-registered gates pass, including stability under paraphrase, a temporal split, a leakage-stripped arm and a missingness ablation.

Why it is not a leakage signature. The gain survives a metadata control capturing note count, note length and author identity (+0.0220, CI +0.0126 to +0.0321), so it is not merely a record of which follow-up group wrote a note. A TF-IDF baseline on the same text scores 0.8766 — below the numeric baseline's 0.9044. Whatever the semantic features capture, bag-of-words does not reach it.

Two label-leakage cautions for anyone applying machine learning to these catalogues. The ExoFOP Comments field restates the disposition in 47.9% of 2,725 labelled rows, where a TF-IDF classifier reaches 0.969 AUC almost entirely from label echo; this is why the study moved to observer notes. Separately, membership in the NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars table predicts the label at P=0.995 versus 0.074, leaking through missingness alone.

Scope, stated rather than implied. The label is a human judgment by the TESS Follow-up Observing Program, and the notes are the evidence record produced on the way to it. This study therefore measures whether a model can anticipate expert consensus from follow-up prose — not whether it can detect planets. The result rests on one corpus, one mission, one snapshot date and one pinned model version (jev-1.13.0), and has not been externally replicated.

On method transparency. The study was designed so that a null result would be publishable. The pre-registered prior predicted a null and was falsified; that is reported rather than dropped. The repository contains the pre-registration, an append-only work log, a full account of a concurrency defect that moved the published headline down by 0.0008, and a measured cold-cache reproduction from a clean machine.

Code is MIT; prose and figures are CC BY 4.0. This research has made use of the Exoplanet Follow-up Observation Program (ExoFOP) and the NASA Exoplanet Archive, both operated by the California Institute of Technology under contract with NASA under the Exoplanet Exploration Program.
